pathophysiology.summary: Cholera is caused by toxigenic Vibrio cholerae O1 or O139 acquired from faecally contaminated water or food. In India it occurs in outbreaks, often in the monsoon and where water and sanitation fail. Cholera toxin activates intestinal adenylate cyclase, causing massive secretion of isotonic fluid and electrolytes into the bowel lumen without mucosal damage. The result is painless, profuse watery ('rice-water') diarrhoea, often with vomiting, that can produce severe dehydration, hypovolaemic shock, metabolic acidosis, hypokalaemia, hypoglycaemia (especially in children) and acute kidney injury within hours. Death is prevented by rapid rehydration: oral rehydration solution (ORS) for no or some dehydration and intravenous Ringer's lactate for severe dehydration, with frequent reassessment. A single dose of antibiotic shortens diarrhoea and shedding in severe or high-risk cases. Zinc is given to young children. Stool culture or polymerase chain reaction (PCR) confirms the diagnosis, but treatment never waits for results.
keyMechanisms: Cholera toxin raises intestinal cyclic AMP, causing secretion of chloride and water.
Isotonic fluid loss causes hypovolaemia, shock and acute kidney injury.
Bicarbonate and potassium loss cause metabolic acidosis and hypokalaemia.
Glucose-coupled sodium absorption stays intact, so ORS works.

pathophysiology.summary: Hepatitis A (HAV) and hepatitis E (HEV) are enterically transmitted hepatotropic viruses spread through contaminated water and food, and cause most acute viral hepatitis in India; HEV causes 10–40% of acute hepatitis and 15–45% of acute liver failure in India and drives waterborne outbreaks. After incubation (HAV about 15–45 days; HEV about 2–10 weeks), immune-mediated hepatocyte injury causes a prodrome of fever, anorexia, nausea and fatigue, followed by dark urine, pale stools and jaundice with alanine aminotransferase (ALT) often more than 10 times normal. Most patients recover with supportive care; there is no antiviral role. A minority develop acute liver failure: encephalopathy within 4 weeks of jaundice with coagulopathy, cerebral oedema and high mortality. Pregnant women with HEV are at particular risk, with case fatality of 10–25%, so symptomatic pregnant women are managed in hospital with intensive care, blood bank and obstetric services.
keyMechanisms: Faecal–oral infection with replication in hepatocytes.
Immune-mediated hepatocyte injury raises transaminases and bilirubin.
Massive necrosis causes acute liver failure with encephalopathy and coagulopathy.
Pregnancy increases the risk of fulminant HEV hepatitis.

pathophysiology.summary: Amoebic liver abscess follows intestinal infection with Entamoeba histolytica acquired from faecally contaminated food or water, which is common in India. Trophozoites invade the colonic mucosa and travel through the portal vein to the liver, where they lyse hepatocytes and form an abscess, usually single and in the right lobe, filled with odourless 'anchovy-paste' fluid. Patients, often young men and especially those who drink alcohol or are malnourished, present with fever and dull right upper abdominal pain, sometimes with cough from diaphragmatic irritation; only a minority have diarrhoea at the time. Ultrasound shows a round hypoechoic lesion, and serology supports the diagnosis. A nitroimidazole cures most patients within 72–96 hours of improvement, followed by a luminal agent to clear gut cysts and prevent relapse. Drainage is reserved for large or left-lobe abscesses, failure to respond, uncertain diagnosis or rupture, which can involve the pleura, lung, pericardium or peritoneum.
keyMechanisms: Invasive trophozoites reach the liver via the portal vein.
Hepatocyte lysis forms an abscess, mostly in the right lobe.
Diaphragmatic irritation and rupture cause cough, pleural, pericardial or peritoneal disease.
Luminal cysts persist after tissue treatment, so a luminal agent is needed.

physicalSigns: Reduced breath sounds at the right base

redFlags: Signs of rupture: peritonitis, pleural effusion, pericarditis or tamponade

pathophysiology.summary: Neurocysticercosis is infection of the central nervous system by the larval stage of the pork tapeworm Taenia solium, acquired by swallowing eggs shed by a human tapeworm carrier through faecally contaminated food, water or hands. It is a leading cause of acquired epilepsy in India, where a single small enhancing lesion is a common presentation. Larvae form cysts in the brain parenchyma, ventricles or subarachnoid space. Viable cysts provoke little reaction; as they degenerate, inflammation and oedema around them cause seizures and headache; calcified lesions can remain seizure foci. Intraventricular and subarachnoid cysts block cerebrospinal fluid flow and cause hydrocephalus and raised intracranial pressure. Management depends on the number, viability and location of cysts on imaging: antiparasitic drugs with corticosteroids for viable cysts and single enhancing lesions, symptomatic treatment alone for calcified disease, and control of intracranial pressure (and neuroendoscopic or shunt surgery) before any antiparasitic therapy when hydrocephalus or diffuse oedema is present.
keyMechanisms: Ingested T. solium eggs release larvae that encyst in brain tissue.
Degenerating cysts trigger perilesional inflammation, causing seizures.
Antiparasitic drugs increase inflammation as cysts die, so steroids are started first.
Ventricular or subarachnoid cysts obstruct cerebrospinal fluid, causing hydrocephalus.

Single enhancing lesion: consider stopping after 6 seizure-free months with lesion resolution; viable cysts: consider tapering after 24 seizure-free months.

pathophysiology.summary: Soil-transmitted helminths — roundworm (Ascaris lumbricoides), whipworm (Trichuris trichiura) and hookworms (Necator americanus and Ancylostoma duodenale) — infect children and adults where sanitation is poor. Eggs in faeces contaminate soil; people swallow eggs on unwashed food or hands, and hookworm larvae penetrate bare feet. Worms feed on blood and tissue and impair absorption, causing iron-deficiency anaemia (especially from hookworm in adolescent girls and women), malnutrition, stunting, impaired cognition and school absence. Heavy roundworm loads can obstruct the bowel or migrate into the bile ducts, and larval migration through the lungs causes Löffler syndrome with cough, wheeze and eosinophilia. India's National Deworming Day gives albendazole twice a year to all children and adolescents aged 1–19 years in schools and anganwadis, with a mop-up day; individual infections are treated with single-dose albendazole, and sanitation, footwear and handwashing prevent reinfection.
keyMechanisms: Faecal contamination of soil spreads eggs; hookworm larvae penetrate skin.
Intestinal blood loss and nutrient malabsorption cause anaemia and malnutrition.
Heavy Ascaris burden causes bowel obstruction or biliary migration.
Larval lung migration causes eosinophilic pneumonitis (Löffler syndrome).

clinicalManagement.title: National Deworming Day
actions: Give albendazole to every child and adolescent aged 1–19 at school or anganwadi; 1–2 years: half tablet crushed with water; 2–19 years: full tablet chewed.
Defer children who are sick or on other medication that day.
Keep children on site for 2 hours; manage mild nausea, vomiting or abdominal pain with rest and water; refer if severe or beyond 24 hours.

clinicalManagement.title: Individual treatment
actions: Albendazole 400 mg single dose; mebendazole is an alternative.
Defer treatment in the early pulmonary phase; repeat after 1–3 months in endemic settings; check household contacts.
WHO includes pregnant women in the second and third trimesters; pyrantel is an option in the first trimester.

clinicalManagement.title: Complications
actions: Bowel obstruction or biliary ascariasis: surgical or endoscopic review.
Treat iron-deficiency anaemia alongside deworming.
